title: Two Sum
description: You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`. Find two different positions whose values add up to `target`, and return their zero-based indices as a list of two integers.
Exactly one pair of positions is guaranteed to work. You may return the indices in either order, but you cannot use the same position twice. Equal values at different positions may form a valid pair.
Return the positions in the original array, rather than the two values. The input is not necessarily sorted.
hints: For each number, what other value would complete the target?
Remember values you have already visited, together with their indices.

examples.explanation: `nums[0] + nums[1]` is `2 + 7 = 9`, so `[0, 1]` is a valid answer. `[1, 0]` is also accepted.
The values at indices `1` and `2` are `2` and `4`. Their sum is `6`.

title: Contains Duplicate
description: You are given an integer array `nums`. Return `True` if there are two different indices containing the same value. Return `False` if every value appears at most once.
Repeated values can occur anywhere in the array; they do not need to be adjacent. Negative numbers and zero are treated like any other integer.
An empty array or an array containing one element has no duplicate, so its answer is `False`.
hints: How could you track values that have already appeared?
Compare the number of distinct values with the array length.

examples.explanation: The value `1` appears at indices `0` and `3`, so the array contains a duplicate.
Each of the four values occurs exactly once.

constraints: Values may be negative or zero.

title: Valid Anagram
description: You are given two strings, `s` and `t`, consisting of lowercase English letters. Return `True` if one string can be rearranged to form the other, and `False` otherwise.
Every occurrence of a letter must be used exactly once. Matching the set of letters is not enough: each letter must appear the same number of times in both strings.
The strings may already be identical. Two empty strings are anagrams of each other; strings of different lengths cannot be anagrams.
hints: Order is irrelevant, but frequency matters.
A frequency table can represent each string.

examples.explanation: Both strings contain three `a` characters and one each of `n`, `g`, `r`, and `m`. Rearranging those letters produces the other string.
`s` contains `t` while `t` contains `c`, so their letter counts differ.

title: Group Anagrams
description: You are given an array of lowercase words, `strs`. Partition the words into groups so that two words belong to the same group exactly when they are anagrams.
Two words are anagrams if their letters can be rearranged to match, using every letter exactly once. Both the letters and their frequencies must agree.

Return a list of groups. The groups may appear in any order, and the words inside each group may appear in any order. Preserve every occurrence from the input, including repeated words and empty strings. For an empty input array, return `[]`.
hints: What representation is identical for all anagrams?
Use that representation as a dictionary key.

examples.explanation: `eat`, `tea`, and `ate` share the same letters; `tan` and `nat` form another group; `bat` has no anagram partner.
The single empty string belongs in its own group. The result contains one group with one word.

constraints: Each word contains up to 100 lowercase English letters.

title: Product of Array Except Self
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return a new array `answer` of the same length. For each index `i`, `answer[i]` must equal the product of all elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`.
Exclude only that one position. If the same value appears elsewhere, its other occurrences still contribute to the product. Inputs may contain negative values and zero, including multiple zeros.
Your algorithm must run in `O(n)` time, where `n = len(nums)`, and must not use division. As an additional space goal, use `O(1)` extra space apart from the returned array.
hints: Split each product into values to the left and to the right.
Can two passes accumulate prefix and suffix products?

examples.explanation: Excluding the first element gives `2 × 3 × 4 = 24`. The remaining positions similarly produce `12`, `8`, and `6`.
Only the position containing zero has a nonzero result: `(-1) × 1 × (-3) × 3 = 9`. Every other product includes zero.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: You are given an unsorted array of integers, `nums`. Return the length of the longest sequence of consecutive integer values present in the array.

Consecutive means that each value is exactly one larger than the previous value, such as `4, 5, 6, 7`. The values may appear in any order and at unrelated positions in the input. You are not looking for a contiguous subarray.
Repeated occurrences of a value do not increase the sequence length. Return `0` for an empty array. Aim for `O(n)` time, where `n = len(nums)`.
hints: Only begin counting at the start of a sequence.
A value starts a sequence if its predecessor is absent.

examples.explanation: The values `1, 2, 3, 4` are all present, giving a sequence of length `4`. The values `100` and `200` do not extend it.
Every integer from `0` through `8` is present, giving length `9`. The repeated `0` is counted only once.

constraints: Values fit in a signed 32-bit integer.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description: You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Return the number of nonempty contiguous subarrays whose elements sum to exactly `k`.

A contiguous subarray consists of all elements between a starting index and an ending index, inclusive. You cannot skip elements. Subarrays with different starting or ending indices count separately, even if they contain identical values, and matching subarrays may overlap.
Values in `nums` and the target `k` may be positive, negative, or zero. Return the number of matches, rather than the subarrays themselves.
hints: Express a subarray sum as the difference of two prefix sums.
Count earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k.

examples.explanation: The subarrays at indices `0..1` and `1..2` both sum to `2`. They overlap but count as two distinct subarrays.
The subarray `[1, 2]` and the single-element subarray `[3]` both sum to `3`.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
description: You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Return the `k` distinct values that occur most frequently in `nums`.

A value's frequency is the number of positions at which it appears. Each selected value must appear once in your answer, regardless of its frequency in the input. You may return the selected values in any order.

The answer set is guaranteed to be unique. When some distinct values are excluded, every selected value has a higher frequency than every excluded value. Ties among selected values are allowed. `k` is at least one and does not exceed the number of distinct input values.
hints: Start by counting occurrences.
A heap or frequency buckets can avoid sorting all the input values.

examples.explanation: `1` appears three times, `2` appears twice, and `3` appears once. The two most frequent values are `1` and `2`.
There is one distinct value, so selecting the most frequent one returns `[1]`.

constraints: The k most frequent values form a unique set.

title: Rotate Image
description: You are given a square `n × n` matrix of integers, `matrix`. Rotate its contents by 90 degrees clockwise.

After rotation, the original top row becomes the rightmost column, read from top to bottom. More generally, a value originally at row `r`, column `c` moves to row `c`, column `n - 1 - r`, using zero-based indices.

Modify the provided matrix in place and return `None`. Do not replace it with a separately returned matrix. The output shown in each example is the state of `matrix` after your function finishes. The rotation must preserve every value, including duplicates.
hints: Think about the effect of a transpose followed by a reflection.
Alternatively rotate four cells at a time, layer by layer.

examples.explanation: The original first row `[1, 2, 3]` becomes the right column. Reading the rotated matrix by rows gives `[7, 4, 1]`, `[8, 5, 2]`, and `[9, 6, 3]`.
The top row `[1, 2]` becomes the right column, and the bottom row `[3, 4]` becomes the left column.

title: Spiral Matrix
description: You are given a rectangular integer matrix `matrix` with `m` rows and `n` columns. Return a one-dimensional list containing every value in clockwise spiral order.

Start at the top-left cell and move right along the top edge. Continue down the right edge, left along the bottom edge, and up the left edge, then continue inward through the remaining cells in the same clockwise direction.

Visit each cell exactly once, including when the remaining region is a single row, a single column, or one cell. The matrix may be rectangular rather than square. Return the visited values in traversal order.
hints: Track the four boundaries of the unvisited rectangle.
After each side, shrink a boundary and check whether any cells remain.

examples.explanation: The outside ring is `1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 8, 7, 4`. The remaining center cell contributes `5`.
The outside ring is `1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 12, 11, 10, 9, 5`. The remaining inner row is `6, 7`.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description: You are given a rectangular integer matrix `matrix`. For every cell that is zero in the original matrix, set all cells in that cell's row and column to zero.
Apply the rule using only the zeros present before any changes. Zeros introduced by your changes must not cause additional rows or columns to be cleared. All other cells keep their original values.

Modify `matrix` in place and return `None`. The example output shows the modified matrix, rather than a return value. A matrix without any zero remains unchanged. As an additional space goal, use constant extra space.
hints: Avoid letting newly written zeros trigger further changes.
The first row and first column can act as markers.

examples.explanation: The original zero is at row `1`, column `1`. That entire row and column become zero; the four corner values remain `1`.
The original zeros are at `(0, 0)` and `(0, 3)`. Clear row `0` and columns `0` and `3`; the middle entries of the other rows remain unchanged.

title: Valid Palindrome
description: You are given a string `s` containing printable ASCII characters. Consider only its letters and digits, and treat uppercase and lowercase versions of a letter as equivalent.

Return `True` if this remaining sequence reads identically from left to right and right to left. Return `False` otherwise. Spaces, punctuation, and symbols do not participate in the comparison, but digits do.
The empty sequence is a palindrome. Therefore, an empty input or a string containing only ignored characters has answer `True`.
hints: Compare the outermost relevant characters.
Skip non-alphanumeric characters as the two pointers move inward.

input.s: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

examples.explanation: After removing spaces and punctuation and ignoring case, the text is `amanaplanacanalpanama`, which reads the same in both directions.
The remaining text is `raceacar`. It differs from its reversal.

title: 3Sum
description: You are given an integer array `nums`. Return all distinct triplets of values whose sum is zero.
Each triplet must come from three different positions in the input. A value may be used more than once within a triplet only if enough separate occurrences exist in `nums`.

Return values, not indices. Two triplets containing the same three values are considered the same answer regardless of their order or the positions used to obtain them. Include each such triplet exactly once. The order of triplets and the order of values inside each triplet do not matter. Return `[]` if no triplet exists.
hints: Sorting makes it easier to avoid duplicates.
Fix one value, then search for the other two with inward-moving pointers.

examples.explanation: The unique value combinations are `-1 + -1 + 2 = 0` and `-1 + 0 + 1 = 0`. Choosing another occurrence of `-1` does not create a new triplet.
The only three available values sum to `2`, so there is no valid triplet.

title: Container With Most Water
description: The nonnegative integers in `height` describe vertical lines at horizontal positions `0` through `len(height) - 1`. Line `i` extends from the x-axis up to height `height[i]`.

Choose two different lines to form the sides of a container, with the x-axis as its base. The water depth is limited by the shorter line, and the width is the distance between the chosen positions. The container must stay upright.

Return the maximum possible area of water, measured as `min(height[i], height[j]) × (j - i)` for `i < j`. Lines between the two selected sides do not reduce this capacity. Return the area, not the chosen indices.
hints: Begin with the widest possible container.
Which pointer can move in a way that might improve the limiting height?

examples.explanation: Choose the lines at indices `1` and `8`, with heights `8` and `7`. Their width is `7` and water depth is `7`, giving area `49`.
The two lines are one unit apart and both have height `1`, so the area is `1`.

title: Trapping Rain Water
description: You are given a list of nonnegative column heights, `height`. Each column has width one, and the columns stand next to each other on a flat baseline in the order shown.

Imagine rain falling until the gaps hold as much water as possible. Water can collect above shorter columns when taller columns contain it on both sides. Water that can escape beyond either outer edge is not retained. The columns themselves occupy solid space.

Return the total amount of trapped water in square units across the entire arrangement. Count water in every enclosed gap, rather than choosing just one pair of columns. If no water can be held, return `0`.
hints: The water above a column is limited by the tallest boundary on each side.
Track the smaller boundary while moving two pointers inward.

examples.explanation: Using zero-based positions, the retained amounts above columns `2`, `4`, `5`, `6`, and `9` are `1`, `1`, `2`, `1`, and `1`. Their total is `6`.
Columns at positions `1`, `2`, and `3` hold `2`, `4`, and `3` units respectively, for a total of `9`.

title: Move Zeroes
description: You are given an integer array `nums`. Move every zero to the end of the same array while keeping all nonzero values in their original relative order.
The array must retain its original length and all of its values. In particular, the number of zeros must stay the same, and negative values count as nonzero values.

Modify `nums` in place and return `None`. Do not return a new array as your answer. The example output shows the contents of `nums` after the modification. Empty arrays and arrays that already have all zeros at the end remain valid.
hints: Keep a write position for the next nonzero value.
After compacting the nonzero values, fill the remaining positions with zeros.

examples.explanation: The nonzero values occur in the order `1, 3, 12`. Keep that order, then place the two zeros after them.
The only value is zero, so the array is already in the required form.

constraints: Modify nums in place; return nothing.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: Given a string `s`, return the length of its longest contiguous substring in which no character appears more than once.

A substring is a consecutive section of the original string. You may choose its starting and ending positions, but you cannot skip characters inside it. Repeated occurrences outside the chosen substring do not matter.

Character comparisons are case-sensitive. Spaces, digits, and punctuation are characters too and must obey the same no-repetition rule. Return the length, not the substring. For an empty string, return `0`.
hints: Maintain a window whose characters are all unique.
When a duplicate arrives, move the left edge past its previous occurrence.

examples.explanation: `abc` is a valid substring of length `3`. Every longer contiguous section contains a repeated character.
Any substring of length greater than `1` repeats `b`, so the longest valid length is `1`.

constraints: Spaces and symbols count as characters.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description: You are given an uppercase English string `s` and a nonnegative integer `k`. You may replace at most `k` characters, changing each selected position to any uppercase English letter.

Return the greatest length of a contiguous substring that can consist entirely of one repeated letter after those replacements. You may choose both the substring and the letter it will contain. Characters outside the chosen substring do not have to match it.

Each changed position costs one replacement, and you do not have to use all `k` replacements. You cannot insert or delete characters, rearrange the string, or combine separate sections into one substring.
hints: A window is feasible when its length minus its most frequent character count is at most k.
Track counts while adjusting the window boundaries.

examples.explanation: Replace the two `B` characters with `A` to obtain `AAAA`. The entire string has length `4`.
The first four characters are `AABA`. Replacing its `B` with `A` gives a matching substring of length `4`; one replacement cannot produce a longer one.

title: Minimum Window Substring
description: You are given strings `s` and `t`. Return the shortest contiguous substring of `s` that contains every character required by `t`, including repeated occurrences.

For example, if `t` contains two `A` characters, a valid window must contain at least two `A` characters. The characters may appear in any order in the window, and the window may also contain extra characters. Matching is case-sensitive.

Return the actual substring from `s`, with its original order and spelling. If no such substring exists, return the empty string `""`. When a valid answer exists, the shortest answer is guaranteed to be unique.
hints: Count the characters still missing from the window.
Once the window covers t, shrink its left edge as far as possible.

examples.explanation: `BANC` contains `A`, `B`, and `C`. No shorter contiguous part of `s` contains all three.
The only character of `s` supplies the only character required by `t`, so the answer is `a`.

constraints: The shortest valid window is unique.

title: Permutation in String
description: You are given two lowercase English strings, `s1` and `s2`. Return `True` if some contiguous substring of `s2` is a permutation of `s1`; otherwise return `False`.

A permutation rearranges all the characters of `s1` without adding or removing any. The matching substring must therefore have exactly `len(s1)` characters and exactly the same number of occurrences of each letter.

The original order of `s1` is allowed as a permutation. Letters elsewhere in `s2` do not count toward the match, and you cannot skip characters within the chosen substring. If `s1` is longer than `s2`, no match is possible.
hints: The candidate window must have exactly len(s1) characters.
Compare the window character frequencies with those of s1.

examples.explanation: `s2` contains the consecutive letters `ba`, which are a rearrangement of `ab`.
Although `a` and `b` both appear, there is no length-two substring containing one of each.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: You are given an integer array `nums` and a window size `k`. A window covers exactly `k` consecutive positions. It starts at index `0` and moves one position right at a time until it reaches the end of the array.
Return an array containing the largest value in each window, ordered by the window's starting position. There are `len(nums) - k + 1` windows, so the answer must have that many entries.

Values may repeat and may be negative. Report maximum values, not their indices. A window of size one reports each original value, while a window covering the whole array produces one result. Aim for `O(n)` time.
hints: Keep only indices that can still become a future maximum.
A decreasing deque discards smaller values at the back and expired indices at the front.

examples.explanation: The six windows have maxima `3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7`. For example, the first window `[1, 3, -1]` has maximum `3`.
There is one window containing the single value `1`.

title: Valid Parentheses
description: You are given a string `s` containing only the six bracket characters `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{`, and `}`. Return whether the brackets form a valid sequence.

Every opening bracket must have a closing bracket of the same type, and every closing bracket must match an earlier opening bracket. Pairs must be correctly nested: a pair opened inside another pair must close before the outer pair closes.

Several complete groups may appear next to each other. For example, `([])` and `()[]` are valid, while `(]` and `([)]` are invalid. A sequence with any unmatched bracket is invalid. The empty string is valid.
hints: The most recent unclosed bracket must close first.
Use a stack, and ensure it is empty at the end.

examples.explanation: The opening parenthesis is followed by its matching closing parenthesis.
The parentheses, square brackets, and braces form three complete groups next to each other.

constraints: Only parentheses, square brackets, and braces appear.

title: Daily Temperatures
description: The array `temperatures` gives the temperature on each day, in chronological order. For every index `i`, find the first later day with a temperature strictly greater than `temperatures[i]`.
Return an integer array of the same length. Its entry at index `i` is the number of days between day `i` and that first warmer day. If no warmer day occurs later, use `0` for that entry.
An equally warm day does not qualify. Count the distance in days, not the increase in temperature, and do not wrap from the end of the array back to the beginning.
hints: Store indices of days still waiting for a warmer temperature.
A new temperature resolves the colder days at the top of a monotonic stack.

examples.explanation: Day `2` has temperature `75`; its next warmer day is day `6` at `76`, so the wait is `4`. The final two days have no later warmer day.
Each day except the last is followed immediately by a warmer day, giving waits `1, 1, 1, 0`.

title: Next Greater Element II
description: You are given an integer array `nums`, treated as circular. After its last position, traversal continues at its first position.

For each index, move forward from the next position and find the first value strictly greater than the value at that index. You may wrap around the array, but stop after considering the other positions once. Equal values do not qualify.

Return an array of these next greater values in the original index order. If an index has no strictly greater value anywhere in the circular traversal, its result is `-1`. Return values rather than indices or distances; the first greater value need not be the largest value.
hints: Simulate a second pass to account for wrapping.
Use a stack of unresolved indices, adding each index only once.

examples.explanation: The first `1` is followed by `2`. The value `2` has no greater value. For the final `1`, wrapping past the first `1` reaches `2`.
The last `3` wraps around and first encounters a greater value at the `4`. The `4` itself has no greater value.

constraints: Values may be negative or repeated.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description: The nonnegative integers in `heights` describe adjacent histogram bars. Each bar is one unit wide and stands on the same horizontal baseline.

Find the greatest area of a rectangle that fits entirely inside the histogram. Its sides must be parallel to the axes, and it must span a contiguous range of bars. Its height cannot exceed any bar within that range.

Return the rectangle's area, not its coordinates. A rectangle may span just one bar or several bars. It may be shorter than some of the bars it covers, but it cannot include space above a shorter bar. If every height is zero, the answer is `0`.
hints: For each bar, locate the nearest smaller bar on either side.
An increasing stack determines a bar’s full width when a shorter bar arrives.

examples.explanation: The adjacent bars of heights `5` and `6` can contain a rectangle of height `5` and width `2`, giving area `10`.
A width-two rectangle of height `2` has area `4`. The single bar of height `4` also gives area `4`.

title: Maximal Rectangle
description: You are given a rectangular binary matrix `matrix`. Each cell contains the string `"0"` or `"1"`, rather than an integer.

Find the largest axis-aligned rectangle made entirely of `"1"` cells and return its area, measured in number of cells. A rectangle uses a consecutive range of rows and a consecutive range of columns; every cell where those ranges intersect must be `"1"`.

The rectangle may be one cell, one row, one column, or a larger block. It does not have to be a square. Cells connected in an irregular shape cannot be counted together as a rectangle. Return `0` if the matrix contains no `"1"` cells.
hints: Treat each row as the base of a histogram of consecutive ones.
Solve a histogram rectangle problem after updating each row’s heights.

examples.explanation: Using zero-based indices, rows `1..2` and columns `2..4` form an all-ones rectangle with `2 × 3 = 6` cells.
The only cell is `"0"`, so there is no all-ones rectangle.

title: Binary Search
description: You are given an integer array `nums` sorted in strictly increasing order, along with an integer `target`. Return the zero-based index at which `target` appears.
If `target` is not present, return `-1`. Every value in `nums` is distinct, so there can be at most one matching position. The target may be smaller than every element or larger than every element.
Your algorithm must run in `O(log n)` time, where `n = len(nums)`. Return the index in the provided array, rather than the matching value or the position where an absent target could be inserted.
hints: Each comparison can discard half the remaining search interval.
Keep your inclusive or exclusive boundary convention consistent.

examples.explanation: The value `9` appears at index `4`, counting from zero.
The array contains no `2`, so the answer is `-1`.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
description: You are given an integer matrix `matrix` with `m` rows and `n` columns, and an integer `target`.

Each row is sorted from left to right in nondecreasing order. In addition, the first value of each row after the first is strictly greater than the final value of the previous row. Thus reading complete rows from top to bottom gives a sorted sequence.
Return `True` if any cell equals `target`, or `False` if it is absent. Return a Boolean, not a row or column index. Your algorithm must run in `O(log(m × n))` time.
hints: The matrix behaves like one sorted array.
Convert a flat index into a row and column with division and remainder.

examples.explanation: `3` occurs in the first row at column `1`, so the answer is `True`.
`13` does not appear in any row of the matrix.

constraints: All rows have equal length and are sorted in nondecreasing order.
Each row after the first starts above the previous row’s final value.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description: You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`. Before it reached you, the array was sorted in strictly increasing order and may have been rotated. All its values are distinct.

A rotation moves a prefix of the sorted array to the end, keeping the order within both parts. For example, `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]` can become `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`. The rotation point is unknown, and an unchanged sorted array is also a valid input.
Return the zero-based index of `target` in the provided, possibly rotated array. If it is absent, return `-1`.
Your algorithm must run in `O(log n)` time, where `n = len(nums)`.
hints: At least one half around the middle is sorted.
Decide whether the target falls inside that sorted half before choosing a side.

examples.explanation: `target` is `0`, which appears at index `4` in the provided array.
The value `3` is absent, so return `-1`.

constraints: nums is an increasing array with a possible rotation.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description: You are given an array `nums` that originally contained distinct integers in strictly increasing order. It may have been rotated by moving a prefix to the end while preserving the order within both parts.
For example, `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` may become `[3, 4, 5, 1, 2]`. You are not given the rotation point. The input may also remain fully sorted, and a one-element array is valid.
Return the smallest value in `nums`, rather than its index. Your algorithm must run in `O(log n)` time, where `n = len(nums)`.
hints: Compare the middle value with the rightmost value.
Determine which side must contain the rotation boundary.

examples.explanation: The sorted values were `1, 2, 3, 4, 5`. Rotation changes their positions but the minimum value is still `1`.
The smallest value in the provided array is `0`.

title: Find First and Last Position
description: You are given an integer array `nums` sorted in nondecreasing order and an integer `target`. Values may repeat.
Return a two-element list containing the zero-based indices of the first and last occurrences of `target`. If it occurs once, both indices are the same. If it does not occur, return `[-1, -1]`.

The input array may be empty, in which case the target is absent. Return positions in the original array, not occurrence counts or insertion positions. Your algorithm must run in `O(log n)` time for a nonempty input of length `n`.
hints: Finding any occurrence is not enough; search for both boundaries.
Use two binary searches with slightly different equality rules.

examples.explanation: The value `8` occupies indices `3` and `4`, which are its first and last positions.
There is no `6` in the array, so both returned positions are `-1`.

constraints: nums is sorted in nondecreasing order.

title: Reverse Linked List
description: You are given `head`, the first node of a singly linked list. Reverse the order of its nodes and return the head of the resulting list.

Each node has a value `val` and a reference `next` to the following node. After reversal, the original last node is first, the original first node is last, and the final node's `next` must be `None`. Preserve all node values and do not create a cycle.
An empty list is represented by `head = None` and should return `None`. A one-node list stays unchanged.
Your function receives `ListNode` objects with `val` and `next` fields, not Python arrays. The examples display node values as arrays; `[]` represents an empty list whose head is `None`.
hints: Keep track of the previous node and the unprocessed suffix.
Save the next pointer before changing the current one.

examples.explanation: Following `next` in the reversed list visits `5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1`, then reaches `None`.
The node containing `2` becomes the head and points to the node containing `1`.

constraints: Each node exposes val and next.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
description: You are given the heads of two singly linked lists, `list1` and `list2`. Each list is sorted in nondecreasing order, meaning equal values may appear next to each other.

Combine their nodes into one singly linked list sorted in the same order, and return its head. Every value occurrence from both inputs must be included exactly once, including duplicates. Reuse the existing nodes where possible.
Either list may be empty. If one is empty, the result contains the other list's values; if both are empty, return `None`.
Your function receives `ListNode` objects with `val` and `next` fields, not Python arrays. The examples display node values as arrays; `[]` represents an empty list whose head is `None`.
hints: A dummy head simplifies appending the next smaller node.
Once one list is exhausted, attach the other list’s remainder.

examples.explanation: Combining the values from both lists in sorted order gives `1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4`. Both occurrences of `1` and `4` are kept.
There are no nodes in either input, so the returned head is `None`, displayed as `[]`.

title: Linked List Cycle
description: You are given `head`, the first node of a singly linked list. Determine whether following its `next` references can eventually revisit the same node. Return `True` if a cycle exists, and `False` if traversal instead reaches `None`.
A cycle is about revisiting a node object. Two separate nodes with equal values do not by themselves form a cycle. An empty list has no cycle; a node that points to itself does.

description: You are given `edges`, a list of undirected connections between nodes labeled `1` through `n`. The graph started as a tree on those nodes, and then one extra edge was added between a pair of distinct nodes that did not already have a direct edge.
A tree is connected and has no cycle. The supplied graph remains connected but has exactly one cycle. Remove one edge so that the remaining graph is again a tree containing all the original nodes.

Return the edge to remove as `[u, v]`. If several edges could be removed successfully, choose the one appearing latest in the provided `edges` list. Preserve the endpoint order used for that edge in the input. The input has `n` nodes and `n` edges.
hints: An edge closes a cycle if its endpoints are already connected.
Use disjoint sets while processing the edges in input order.

examples.explanation: All three edges form a triangle. Removing any one breaks the cycle, and `[2, 3]` occurs last in the input.
The cycle uses nodes `1, 2, 3, 4`. Its latest listed edge is `[1, 4]`. The later edge `[1, 5]` is not on that cycle and cannot be removed instead.

constraints: Node labels range from 1 to n.
The input has exactly one cycle.

title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
description: You are given a square integer matrix `grid`. A cell containing `0` is open, and a cell containing `1` is blocked.

Find the shortest path from the top-left cell `(0, 0)` to the bottom-right cell `(n - 1, n - 1)`. Every visited cell, including both endpoints, must be open. Each move may go to any of the eight neighboring cells sharing an edge or corner, and must stay inside the grid.

Return the path length measured in visited cells, including the starting cell. If no valid path exists, return `-1`. A one-cell grid containing `0` has path length `1`; a blocked endpoint makes a path impossible.
hints: All moves have the same cost, so breadth-first search finds a shortest path.
Check both endpoints and mark cells when enqueuing them.

examples.explanation: Move diagonally from `(0,0)` to `(1,1)`. Both cells are open, so the path visits two cells.
One shortest path is `(0,0) → (0,1) → (1,2) → (2,2)`, visiting four open cells.

title: Climbing Stairs
description: A staircase has `n` steps. You begin on the ground below the first step, and each move takes you upward by either one step or two steps.

Return the number of distinct sequences of moves that land exactly on step `n`. You cannot overshoot the top. The order of moves matters: taking one step and then two steps is a different sequence from taking two steps and then one step.
Return the count, not the sequences themselves. For a staircase of one step, the only possible sequence is a single one-step move.
hints: Your final move comes from one step below or two steps below.
The two previous counts are enough to compute the next count.

examples.explanation: There are two sequences: `1 + 1` and `2`.
There are three sequences: `1 + 1 + 1`, `1 + 2`, and `2 + 1`.

title: House Robber
description: The nonnegative integers in `nums` describe the amount of money in houses arranged in a straight line. You may take money from any set of houses, provided you do not choose two adjacent houses.

Return the greatest total amount you can take. Houses at consecutive indices are adjacent, so choosing index `i` prevents choosing `i - 1` and `i + 1` when those positions exist. Each house can be chosen at most once.
The first and last houses are not neighbors unless they are next to each other in the line. You may skip any number of houses. Return the maximum amount, not the selected house indices.
hints: At each position, compare skipping it with taking it plus the best result two positions earlier.
Only the previous two best results are needed.

examples.explanation: Choose houses at indices `0` and `2`, with amounts `1` and `3`. They are not adjacent and total `4`.
Choose indices `0`, `2`, and `4`, giving `2 + 9 + 1 = 12`.

title: House Robber II
description: The nonnegative integers in `nums` describe money in houses arranged in a circle. You may take money from houses as long as no two chosen houses are adjacent.

Consecutive indices are neighbors, and the final house is also next to the first house. For two or more houses, you therefore cannot choose both the first and last. Each chosen house contributes its amount once.

Return the largest total amount possible. With just one house, you may choose that house; it does not conflict with itself. You may leave any house unchosen, and a circle containing only zero amounts has answer `0`.
hints: A valid choice cannot include both endpoints.
Compare the best answer excluding the first value with the best answer excluding the last.

examples.explanation: The first and last houses are neighbors, so their two amounts of `2` cannot both be taken. Choosing the middle house gives the best total, `3`.
Choose indices `0` and `2` for `1 + 3 = 4`. These houses are not adjacent in the circle.

title: Coin Change
description: You are given positive coin denominations in `coins` and a nonnegative integer `amount`. You have an unlimited supply of coins of each listed denomination.

Return the smallest number of coins whose values sum to exactly `amount`. You may use a denomination repeatedly and may ignore other denominations. If no collection of the available coins can form the exact amount, return `-1`.
The order of chosen coins does not affect the result; you are minimizing the total number of coins. When `amount` is zero, no coins are needed, so return `0`.
hints: Build the best answer for smaller amounts.
For each amount, try every possible final coin.

examples.explanation: Use coins `5 + 5 + 1 = 11`, for three coins. No choice of fewer coins reaches `11`.
Any sum of coins worth `2` is even, so the amount `3` cannot be formed.

title: Coin Change II
description: You are given a nonnegative integer `amount` and distinct positive denominations in `coins`. An unlimited supply of each denomination is available.

Return the number of different combinations of coins that add up to exactly `amount`. A combination is determined by the number of coins of each denomination, so choosing the same coins in a different order does not create another combination.
You may use any denomination zero or more times. Return `0` when the positive amount cannot be formed. For `amount = 0`, return `1`: choosing no coins is the single valid combination.
hints: Process denominations in the outer loop to count combinations instead of sequences.
Each denomination adds ways to amounts that can use it.

examples.explanation: The four combinations are `5`, `2 + 2 + 1`, `2 + 1 + 1 + 1`, and `1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1`.
Using only coins of value `2` cannot produce `3`, so there are zero combinations.

constraints: Coin values are positive and distinct.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description: You are given an integer array `nums`. Return the length of its longest strictly increasing subsequence.

A subsequence is formed by deleting zero or more elements while preserving the relative order of the elements that remain. The selected values do not have to be adjacent, but they cannot be rearranged.

Strictly increasing means every selected value after the first is greater than the previous selected value; equal values cannot extend the sequence. Return only the maximum length. A nonempty array always has a subsequence of length one. Use O(n log n) time for this speedrun.
hints: For subsequences of the same length, a smaller ending value leaves more room for future elements.
Maintain the smallest possible tail for each length. These tails stay sorted, so use binary search to find where each new value belongs.

examples.explanation: One longest subsequence is `[2, 3, 7, 101]`, of length `4`. `[2, 3, 7, 18]` is another with the same length.
The values at indices `0, 1, 4, 5` form `[0, 1, 2, 3]`, a strictly increasing subsequence of length `4`.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
description: You are given two lowercase strings, `text1` and `text2`. Return the length of the longest sequence of characters that is a subsequence of both strings.

A subsequence may skip characters, but it preserves the relative order of every character it keeps. The characters need not be consecutive. Each occurrence in an input can be used at most once in that string's subsequence.
The selected sequence must be identical in both strings. Return its maximum possible length, rather than the sequence itself. If the strings have no common character, return `0`.
hints: When the current characters match, they can extend a shorter common subsequence.
Otherwise compare skipping a character from either string.

examples.explanation: `ace` appears in order in both strings. It has length `3`, and no longer sequence can fit in `text2`.
The strings are identical, so their entire length-three text is a common subsequence.

title: Word Break
description: You are given a nonempty lowercase string `s` and an array of nonempty dictionary words, `wordDict`. Return whether `s` can be divided into one or more consecutive pieces, each of which is a dictionary word.

Every character of `s` must be covered exactly once, in its original order. Pieces must meet without gaps or overlap. You may reuse a dictionary word any number of times, and you do not have to use every dictionary entry.
Return `True` if at least one complete segmentation exists, and `False` otherwise. A dictionary word matching all of `s` is a valid one-piece segmentation.
hints: Mark which prefixes can be fully segmented.
A reachable prefix can be extended by any matching dictionary word.

examples.explanation: Split the text into `leet` followed by `code`; both pieces are dictionary words.
The split `apple` + `pen` + `apple` covers the whole string. Reusing `apple` is allowed.

constraints: Dictionary entries are nonempty lowercase words.
A dictionary word may be used more than once.

title: Unique Paths
description: You are on the top-left cell of a rectangular grid with `m` rows and `n` columns. The destination is the bottom-right cell.
On each move, you may travel exactly one cell to the right or one cell downward. You cannot move left or up, leave the grid, or skip cells. There are no blocked cells.

Return the number of distinct paths from the start to the destination. Paths are different when their sequences of moves differ. A grid with one row or one column has exactly one path; a one-cell grid also has one path, requiring no moves.
hints: A cell can be reached only from above or from the left.
The top row and left column each have exactly one path.

examples.explanation: Reaching the destination requires two downward moves and six rightward moves. There are `28` different orders for those moves.
The paths use the move sequences down-down-right, down-right-down, and right-down-down, giving `3`.

constraints: The answer fits in a signed 32-bit integer.

title: Decode Ways
description: The numbers `1` through `26` encode the letters `A` through `Z`, respectively. You are given a nonempty string `s` containing only decimal digits. Return how many ways it can be decoded into letters.

A decoding splits the entire string into consecutive one- or two-digit codes. Each code must represent a number from `1` to `26`. Every digit must be used once, in order, and a code must not start with `0`.
Thus `10` and `20` are valid codes, but `0`, `06`, and `30` are not. Different valid splits count as different decodings. Return `0` if no complete decoding exists.
hints: A valid final code uses either one digit or two digits.
Handle zero carefully: it is never a valid one-digit code.

examples.explanation: `12` can be split as `1 | 2` to give `AB`, or kept as `12` to give `L`, for two decodings.
The valid splits are `2 | 2 | 6` (`BBF`), `22 | 6` (`VF`), and `2 | 26` (`BZ`).

constraints: Leading zeros cannot form a valid code.

title: Edit Distance
description: You are given two strings, `word1` and `word2`. Return the minimum number of operations needed to transform `word1` into `word2` exactly.

One operation may insert a single character at any position, delete a single character, or replace a single character with another character. Each operation costs one. Swapping adjacent characters is not a separate allowed operation.

Both strings may be empty. If they are already identical, the cost is zero. Transforming an empty string into a nonempty one requires inserting every character, and transforming a nonempty string into an empty one requires deleting every character. Return only the minimum cost.
hints: Define the cost of converting each prefix of one word into a prefix of the other.
A mismatch offers three operations; take the cheapest predecessor state.

examples.explanation: One three-operation transformation is `horse → rorse → rose → ros`: replace `h`, delete the extra `r`, then delete `e`.
One five-operation transformation is `intention → inention → enention → exention → exection → execution`: one deletion, three replacements, and one insertion.

constraints: Each allowed operation has unit cost.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
description: You are given an integer array `nums`. Return the largest product obtainable by multiplying the elements of one nonempty contiguous subarray.
A subarray is a consecutive section of the input; you cannot skip elements inside it or combine separated sections. It may consist of a single element or the entire array.
Values may be positive, negative, or zero. Multiplication uses their signed values, and an empty product is not an allowed answer. Return the product itself, rather than the subarray or its indices.
hints: A negative value can turn the smallest product into the largest.
Track both the maximum and minimum product ending at the current position.

examples.explanation: The contiguous subarray `[2, 3]` has product `6`, the greatest possible product for this input.
The subarray `[0]` has product `0`. The two negative values cannot be combined without also including the zero between them.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
description: You are given a nonempty string `s`. Return a longest contiguous substring of `s` that is a palindrome.

A palindrome reads identically forward and backward. A substring consists of consecutive characters from the original string, so you cannot skip or rearrange characters. Comparisons are exact and case-sensitive; no characters are removed before checking.

Return the substring itself. If several palindromic substrings tie for the greatest length, any one of them is accepted. A single character is always a palindrome, so every allowed input has an answer.
hints: Every palindrome has a center: either a character or a gap.
Expand around each possible center while the two sides match.

examples.explanation: Both `bab` and `aba` are palindromic substrings of length `3`. Either is accepted, and no longer palindrome exists.
`bb` is the longest palindromic substring, with length `2`.

constraints: Return any longest palindrome if there is a tie.

title: Palindromic Substrings
description: Given a nonempty string `s`, return the number of its nonempty contiguous substrings that are palindromes.
A palindrome reads identically forward and backward using exact, case-sensitive character comparisons. Single-character substrings qualify. You cannot skip characters when choosing a substring.

Count occurrences by their starting and ending positions. Two occurrences with the same text count separately if they occupy different positions, and overlapping occurrences are allowed. Return the total count, rather than the distinct palindrome texts.
hints: Expand around every possible odd and even center.
Each successful expansion contributes one palindrome.

examples.explanation: The three one-character substrings `a`, `b`, and `c` are palindromes. No longer substring qualifies.
There are three occurrences of `a`, two occurrences of `aa`, and one occurrence of `aaa`, totaling `6`.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
description: You are given an array of positive integers, `nums`. Return whether all its elements can be split into two groups with equal total sums.

Every input occurrence must belong to exactly one group. You cannot discard elements, use an occurrence twice, or split a value. Values at different positions count as separate occurrences even when they are equal.

The groups do not need to be contiguous and may contain different numbers of elements. Return `True` if any equal-sum partition exists, or `False` otherwise. Return a Boolean, not the groups themselves.
hints: An odd total makes a partition impossible.
Otherwise, ask whether a subset can reach half of the total.

examples.explanation: One group contains `[1, 5, 5]` and the other contains `[11]`. Both sum to `11`.
The values sum to `11`, so they cannot be divided into two groups with equal integer sums.

title: Maximum Subarray
description: You are given an integer array `nums`. Return the greatest sum obtainable from one nonempty contiguous subarray.
A subarray is a consecutive section of the input. It may contain one element, several neighboring elements, or the entire array, but you cannot skip values inside it.

Values may be negative or zero, and the input may contain only negative numbers. You must still select at least one element in that case; choosing an empty subarray with sum zero is not allowed. Return the maximum sum rather than the selected elements or their indices.
hints: At each position, either extend the previous subarray or start a new one.
Keep the best answer seen separately from the best answer ending here.

examples.explanation: The contiguous section `[4, -1, 2, 1]` has sum `6`, which is the greatest possible sum.
The only nonempty subarray is `[1]`, so the result is `1`.

title: Jump Game
description: You are given a nonempty array of nonnegative integers, `nums`, and start at index `0`. From index `i`, you may jump forward by any whole number of positions from `1` through `nums[i]`, provided you remain within the array.
The value is a maximum jump length; you do not have to jump the full amount. A zero permits no forward move from that position. You may jump over positions without visiting them.
Return `True` if you can reach the final index, and `False` otherwise. If the array has one element, you already occupy the final index and the answer is `True`, even when that element is zero.
hints: Track the farthest position reachable so far.
If the current index exceeds that frontier, progress is impossible.

examples.explanation: Jump from index `0` to `1`, then from index `1` to `4`. The jump lengths `1` and `3` are permitted.
Every route from the start is confined to indices `0..3`. The zero at index `3` cannot move you to the last index `4`.

title: Jump Game II
description: You start at index `0` of a nonempty array of nonnegative integers, `nums`. At index `i`, you may jump forward by any integer distance from `1` through `nums[i]`, landing on an index inside the array.
Return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the final index. A jump may be shorter than the maximum allowed distance, and each jump counts as one regardless of its length.
The input guarantees that the last index is reachable. With one element, you are already there and must return `0`. Return only the number of jumps, not the visited positions.
hints: Think of positions reachable with the same number of jumps as a layer.
When the current layer ends, advance to the farthest next frontier.

examples.explanation: Jump from index `0` to `1`, then to index `4`. This takes two jumps; the first position cannot reach index `4` directly.
The route `0 → 1 → 4` still works in two jumps, so the zero at index `2` does not need to be visited.

title: Merge Intervals
description: You are given an array of closed intervals, `intervals`, where `[start, end]` includes both endpoints. The intervals are not necessarily sorted.

Merge all overlapping intervals so that the result contains mutually nonoverlapping intervals covering exactly the same set of points as the input. Intervals that share an endpoint overlap: `[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]` must merge into `[1, 5]`.

Overlaps can connect a chain of several intervals, and an interval fully contained in another does not create an extra output interval. Return the merged intervals in any order, with each interval's start before or equal to its end.
hints: Sort intervals by starting position.
Compare the next start with the end of the current merged interval.

examples.explanation: `[1, 3]` and `[2, 6]` overlap and combine into `[1, 6]`. The intervals `[8, 10]` and `[15, 18]` remain separate.
Both intervals contain the endpoint `4`, so they merge into `[1, 5]`.

title: Insert Interval
description: You are given closed intervals in `intervals`, already sorted by their starting values and mutually nonoverlapping. You are also given one closed interval, `newInterval`.
Add `newInterval` to the covered range and merge every overlap it creates, so the result is again sorted by start and nonoverlapping. Closed intervals that meet at an endpoint overlap and must merge.

Return the resulting list of intervals. You do not have to modify the original list in place. Existing intervals that remain disjoint must keep their original endpoints. If `intervals` is empty, return a list containing only `newInterval`.
hints: Separate intervals before, overlapping, and after the new interval.
Expand the new interval as you encounter overlaps.

examples.explanation: `[2, 5]` overlaps `[1, 3]`, creating `[1, 5]`. It does not reach `[6, 9]`, which stays separate.
`[4, 8]` overlaps `[3, 5]` and `[6, 7]`, and meets `[8, 10]`. Together they form `[3, 10]`; the outside intervals remain unchanged.

constraints: Existing intervals are sorted and nonoverlapping.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
description: You are given a collection of intervals, `intervals`, each written as `[start, end]` with `start < end`. Return the minimum number of intervals that must be removed so the remaining intervals do not overlap.
For this problem, intervals that only share an endpoint are compatible. For example, `[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]` can both remain. Intervals overlap when they share a range of positive length.

You may remove whole intervals, but cannot shorten or move them. Repeated identical intervals count as separate input entries, so overlapping duplicates may need to be removed. Return the number removed, not the number retained or the intervals themselves.
hints: Prefer keeping the interval that finishes earliest.
This leaves the most room for future intervals.

examples.explanation: Remove `[1, 3]`. The remaining `[1, 2]`, `[2, 3]`, and `[3, 4]` touch only at endpoints, so one removal is enough.
At most one of the three identical intervals can remain. Remove the other two.

constraints: Intervals that only touch do not overlap.

title: Single Number
description: You are given a nonempty integer array `nums`. Exactly one value occurs once, while every other distinct value occurs exactly twice.
Return the value that occurs once. The repeated occurrences may be anywhere in the array, and values may be negative or zero. The input is not necessarily sorted.
Your algorithm must run in `O(n)` time and use `O(1)` extra space, where `n = len(nums)`. Return the unique value itself, not its index. For a one-element array, that element is the answer.
hints: Which bitwise operation cancels a value with itself?
The order of XOR operations does not affect the result.

examples.explanation: `2` appears twice and `1` appears once, so return `1`.
`1` and `2` each appear twice. The value `4` is the only value appearing once.

constraints: One value occurs once; every other value occurs twice.

title: Counting Bits
description: You are given a nonnegative integer `n`. Return an array `answer` of length `n + 1`, where `answer[i]` is the number of `1` digits in the binary representation of `i`.
Include every integer from `0` through `n`, inclusive, in that order. Leading zeros do not affect a bit count. In particular, the value zero has no set bits, so `answer[0]` is `0`.
Return the individual counts, not their sum or the binary strings. For example, `5` is written `101` in binary and has two set bits.
hints: Relate a number’s bits to those of the number shifted right once.
Alternatively, remove its lowest set bit and reuse that earlier count.

examples.explanation: The values `0, 1, 2` have binary representations `0, 1, 10`, with counts `0, 1, 1`.
The representations for `0..5` are `0, 1, 10, 11, 100, 101`, producing counts `0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2`.

title: Number of 1 Bits
description: You are given an integer `n` in the unsigned 32-bit range, from `0` through `2³² - 1`. Return how many of its binary digits are `1`; this count is also called its Hamming weight.

Treat `n` as a numeric value, not a string of decimal digits. Leading zero bits do not contribute to the answer. For example, decimal `11` has binary representation `1011` and contains three `1` bits.
Zero has no set bits, so its answer is `0`. Return the count as an integer.
hints: Check the lowest bit, then shift.
The expression n & (n − 1) removes the lowest set bit.

examples.explanation: Decimal `11` is `1011` in binary. Three positions contain a `1`.
Decimal `128` is `10000000` in binary, which contains one `1`.

title: Missing Number
description: You are given an array `nums` of length `n` containing distinct integers selected from the inclusive range `0` through `n`. Exactly one value from that range is missing.
Return the missing value. The array need not be sorted, and the missing value may be `0`, `n`, or any value between them. No input value is duplicated or outside the stated range.
The range contains `n + 1` possible values while the input contains `n` of them. For an empty array, `n = 0`, the range consists only of zero, and the answer is `0`.
hints: Compare the expected aggregate of 0 through n with the actual values.
Either an arithmetic sum or XOR can use constant extra space.

examples.explanation: With three input values, the full range is `0, 1, 2, 3`. The missing value is `2`.
With two input values, the full range is `0, 1, 2`. The array contains `0` and `1`, so return `2`.

constraints: Values are distinct and in [0, len(nums)].

title: Implement Trie
description: Implement the class `Trie` to store lowercase English words and answer word and prefix queries. A newly constructed `Trie()` starts empty, and the same instance must retain inserted words across subsequent method calls.
`insert(word)` adds the complete word to the trie and returns `None`. Inserting an already stored word leaves it stored; it does not change the meaning of searches.
`search(word)` returns `True` only when that exact complete word has previously been inserted. A word that is merely a prefix of a longer stored word does not count as inserted.

`startsWith(prefix)` returns `True` when at least one inserted word begins with every character of `prefix`, in order. A complete stored word is also a prefix of itself. Return `False` when no stored word matches.

Each test supplies parallel arrays `operations` and `arguments`. The runner creates one empty `Trie`, then invokes `operations[i]` with `arguments[i]` in sequence. Implement the class methods, not a function taking these arrays. The displayed output records each method's return value; `null` represents Python `None`.
hints: Share nodes for words with a common prefix.
A node needs children and a marker distinguishing a complete word from a prefix.

examples.explanation: After inserting `apple`, searching `apple` succeeds, searching `app` fails, and checking prefix `app` succeeds. Inserting `app` makes the final exact search succeed. The insert calls return `None`.
After inserting `cat`, `dog` is not a stored word, while `ca` is a prefix of `cat`.

constraints: 1 ≤ length of each word or prefix ≤ 2,000
All arguments contain lowercase English letters.
